title: Getting started
summary: What Woodshop is and the ways to start your first design.

blocks.text: Woodshop turns a furniture idea into a real, buildable design: a 3D model you can spin around, plus an automatic cut list of every board to buy and cut. Everything runs on this computer — there is no account, no subscription, and nothing leaves your machine unless you export it.
Ways to start

items: Start from a template. The Templates gallery has ready-made designs (side table, bookshelf, workbench, and more). Pick one and it opens in the editor as your own copy.
Start blank. Create a project and build it up part by part from the Add menu.
Import a file. Open a .woodshop project someone sent you (or double-click it), or a spec JSON exported from the web version of Woodshop.
Let your own AI agent build it. Connect Claude Desktop or Claude Code over MCP (see Connect your own AI agent) and describe what you want.

blocks.text: How a design is stored

Every design is a set of parts, materials, and joints — measured in inches. Woodshop draws the 3D model and the cut list from that description, so the two are always in sync. You never edit raw 3D shapes; you change the design and everything updates.
Your projects live in a single library on this computer. Use Export… on a project to save a .woodshop file for backup or to move it to another machine.

title: The 3D editor
summary: Move, resize, and join parts; undo and version history.

blocks.text: The editor is where you see and shape a design. The 3D view shows the assembled piece; the inspector shows the selected part and its dimensions.
Working with parts

items: Select a part to see its size, material, and position in the inspector.
Resize a part by editing its length and width. Thickness comes from the material.
Move or rotate a part to position it.

blocks.text: Joinery

Woodshop detects joints — dado, pocket-hole, screwed, and dowel — where parts meet, and records them on the design. Joints are annotations that describe how pieces connect; moving a part never secretly moves its neighbours.

Touching is not holding. A part that only rests against its neighbours is flagged as unbuildable until something fastens it: pick the part, then use "Fasten to" in the inspector for pocket screws, screws through the face, or dowels. Woodshop sizes the screws for the thicknesses involved and adds them to the hardware list on your cut list.
Undo and safety
Every change can be undone. Your work autosaves as you go, and you can save named versions to go back to (see Versions & autosave).
The 3D view has two modes: View (orbit and zoom the camera only) and Edit (select, drag and change parts). Switch with the Edit/View toggle in the toolbar so a drag does what you expect.

title: Cut lists & materials
summary: Every board to cut, board feet, sheet layouts, and a printable plan.

blocks.text: The cut list is generated from your design — it is always up to date. It lists every part, how many to cut, its dimensions, and the material.
What it shows

items: Parts table: each part, quantity, dimensions in inches, and board feet.
Sheet goods (plywood, MDF): how many sheets and how the parts are laid out to minimise waste, grain-aware.
Lumber: how the parts are cut from stock lengths.
Totals: board feet, sheet count, estimated cost, and waste.

blocks.text: Cutting allows for a saw kerf (the width of material the blade removes) between pieces, so the plan reflects what you can really get out of a sheet or board.
Printable plan
Export a PDF plan to take to the shop or the lumberyard — it includes the parts table and layouts.
A connected AI agent can fetch the parts table and board feet with the `get_cut_list` tool; the full packed sheet layout lives here in the app.

title: Adding hardware
summary: Pulls, hinges, slides, casters and more: real sizes, shown in 3D and counted in the hardware list.

blocks.text: Woodshop has a catalog of real hardware with true dimensions: knobs and pulls, hinges, drawer slides, casters, leveling feet, brackets and plates, shelf pins, latches, lid stays and handles, and hooks. Hardware shows in the 3D view, moves with the part it is screwed to, and is counted in the hardware list, so the cut list, PDF and CSV tell you what to buy.
Put hardware on a part

items: Open Add ▸ Hardware… in the editor toolbar, or select a part and choose + Add hardware in the inspector.
Pick a category or search, and click an item to see a preview and its size.
Choose Place on the model, then click where it goes on a part's face. Press R to turn it a quarter turn. You can keep clicking to place more; press Esc or Done when you are finished.
Or pick a part under "Or add to the centre of" and choose Add to drop it in the middle of that part's front face.

blocks.text: Move, turn or remove it

Click a piece in the 3D view, or select its part, to see it in the inspector's Hardware section. There you can change which side it is on (front or back face, an edge, or an end), type its position in inches, turn it 90°, or remove it. Casters and feet usually go on an end: the end of a leg or the bottom edge of a base.
Doors and drawers

A door's hinges and pull, and a drawer's slides and pull, are chosen on the door or drawer itself: select its part and use the Hinge, Slides and Pull pickers in the Door / Drawer section. Woodshop places them for you and moves them as the door swings or the drawer slides. Choose None for a push latch or a wooden pull.

Hardware never cuts the part. If a piece needs a hole (a cup for a concealed hinge, a hole for a pull's screws), add a hole from the inspector's cuts. Casters and feet do add to the overall height shown in the cut list.

title: Versions & autosave
summary: How your work is saved, and how to go back to an earlier design.

blocks.text: You do not need to hit save. The editor autosaves your working design a moment after you stop making changes, and reopening a project restores exactly where you left off.
Version history

items: Save a version to bookmark a design you like before experimenting.
Before a connected AI agent changes a design, Woodshop snapshots your current design automatically — labelled so you can find it.
Restore any earlier version to roll back; restoring makes it your current working design.

blocks.text: If an AI agent edits the project you have open, the editor picks the change up. If you had unsaved edits at the same moment, Woodshop asks whether to keep yours or take the other, so nothing is silently lost.

title: Connect your own AI agent
summary: Let Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or another MCP client build in Woodshop for you.

blocks.text: Woodshop includes an MCP server that runs on this computer, so your own AI agent (Claude Desktop, Claude Code, an IDE assistant, or something you build) can list, read, create, and edit your designs. No account or token is needed — the server only ever talks to the library on this machine.
Set it up

items: Open Settings → AI agents (MCP) and copy the configuration shown there.
Paste it into your MCP client's configuration (for Claude Desktop: Settings → Developer → Edit Config). It launches Woodshop with `--mcp` as a local stdio server.
Restart the client. Ask it to `list_projects` to check the connection.

blocks.text: What the agent can do

items: Read: `list_projects`, `get_design`, `get_cut_list`, `check_design`, `explain_part`.
Start: `start_design` (a blank design) or `start_from_template`.
Exact edits: `add_part`, `resize_part`, `move_part`, `add_op`, `add_joint`, `set_material`, `delete_part`, and more — every edit is validated against the same rules as the editor.

blocks.text: Every agent edit is saved as a version first, so you can always restore what you had. The agent works on your library even while the app is closed.

title: Shop calculators
summary: Fourteen calculators for the numbers you work out at the bench — no project needed.

blocks.text: Everything else in Woodshop works from a design. The calculators do not: they take numbers you type and hand back an answer, so you can reach for them with nothing open. Find them under **Tools**, or from the ⋯ menu in the editor toolbar while you are working.
Typing measurements

Every dimension field reads fractions the way you write them: `3/4`, `1 1/2`, `1-1/2`, or plain decimals like `12.5`. Nothing complains while you are mid-word — `1 1/` is part of typing `1 1/2` — and when you leave the field it tidies what you typed, so `0.375` becomes `3/8`. Where a field offers units, switching converts the value rather than the digits.
What is here

items: **Material & stock** — board feet and cost for a pile of rough lumber; how many boards or sheets your parts cut from, kerf included; and a converter that also shows how far your fraction rounds off.
**Strength & seasonal movement** — whether a shelf will sag under load and the longest span that still passes; and how much a solid panel grows and shrinks between winter and summer.
**Joinery** — mortise and tenon proportions, dowel size and spacing, and pilot, clearance and countersink sizes for a screw in your species.
**Angles, curves & proportion** — saw settings for any number of sides (flat or canted), arcs from a chord and rise, segmented rings, leg tapers and splays, and proportion helpers.

blocks.text: They agree with the rest of the app

The shelf-sag calculator uses the same maths as the sturdiness warnings in the editor, and the pilot-hole calculator sizes screws with the same rules that draw them on your design. So a calculator will never tell you something different from what the editor tells you about the same shelf or the same joint.
They never touch your project

The calculators do not read your design and cannot change it. Opening them from the editor puts them over the canvas without navigating away — your selection, camera and undo history are exactly where you left them when you close it.
A stock estimate counts the saw kerf between every cut, which is why two 48-inch pieces do not come out of one 96-inch board.
